subject: Science
learning_objectives: Describe the history and discovery of magnets
Identify magnetic and non-magnetic materials with examples
Explain the properties of a bar magnet — poles, attraction, repulsion
Understand how a freely suspended magnet always points north–south
Describe how to find the poles of a magnet using another magnet
Explain how a compass works and its use in navigation
Describe methods of making a temporary magnet
Understand how magnets lose their magnetic properties
Connect magnetism to everyday technology and Karnataka examples
prerequisite_knowledge: Basic awareness of metals and non-metals from everyday life
Understanding that some objects attract each other (e.g. sticky tape)
Familiarity with the concept of force from daily experience

introduction.why_important: Magnets are everywhere — in speakers, MRI machines, electric motors, compasses, and refrigerator doors. Understanding magnetism is the foundation for understanding electricity and many modern technologies. It is one of the four fundamental forces in nature.
introduction.real_life_relevance: Every time you stick a note on a refrigerator, use a speaker, or check direction on your phone, you are using magnetism. Electric motors in fans, pumps, and vehicles all work because of magnetic principles.
introduction.karnataka_context: Karnataka has significant iron ore deposits in Bellary (now Ballari) and Chitradurga districts — iron being the classic magnetic material. NMDC (National Mineral Development Corporation), headquartered in Hyderabad but with major operations in Karnataka, mines iron ore that is used in steel making. The Indian Institute of Science (IISc) in Bengaluru conducts world-class research in materials science and magnetism. ISRO's satellite guidance systems in Bengaluru use magnetic sensors. Belagavi and Hubballi have industrial units manufacturing electromagnets and motors.
introduction.connection_to_previous_learning: Students have learned about materials and their properties in earlier chapters. This chapter extends that by exploring a special property — magnetism — shown by certain materials.

characters.role: The central object — a material that attracts iron, nickel, and cobalt and has two poles

characters.name: Magnetic Needle / Compass
characters.role: A freely suspended magnet that always aligns north–south — used for navigation for centuries

characters.name: Magnetic and Non-magnetic Materials

plot: The chapter opens with the story of Magnes, a shepherd from ancient Greece, whose iron-tipped staff stuck to a rock (lodestone/magnetite) — the legendary discovery of magnetism.
Students explore which materials are attracted by a magnet (magnetic: iron, nickel, cobalt) and which are not (non-magnetic: wood, plastic, rubber, glass, aluminium).
The chapter introduces the concept of magnetic poles — the two ends of a magnet (North and South poles) where the magnetic force is strongest.
It explains the law of magnetic poles: like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
A freely suspended bar magnet always aligns in the north–south direction — this is used in compasses for navigation.
Students learn how to find the poles of an unmarked magnet using a known magnet.
The chapter covers how to make temporary magnets by stroking with a magnet or using electricity (electromagnets).
It explains how magnets lose their properties when heated, dropped, or hammered.
story_summary.moral: Simple natural phenomena like magnetism, when understood deeply, power the technologies that run our modern world.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: Some materials are attracted to magnets (magnetic materials) and some are not (non-magnetic materials). Only a few metals are magnetic.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Magnetic materials are those attracted to a magnet. The main magnetic materials are iron, nickel, and cobalt (and their alloys like steel). Non-magnetic materials include wood, plastic, rubber, glass, paper, copper, aluminium, and most non-metals. A common misconception is that all metals are magnetic — aluminium, copper, gold, and silver are metals but are non-magnetic. The test for magnetism is simple: bring a magnet near the object. If the object is attracted, it is magnetic.
core_concepts.real_life_example: Test objects in your pencil box: a steel geometry box lid will be attracted to a magnet, but an aluminium ruler will not. A steel pin will stick to a magnet, but a copper coin will not.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Iron ore mines in Ballari (formerly Bellary) district of Karnataka produce magnetite (Fe₃O₄) — a naturally occurring magnetic rock also known as lodestone. These deposits are among the largest in India. Steel plants using Karnataka iron ore produce steel — a magnetic material used in everything from utensils to bridges.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students assume all metals are magnetic. Aluminium, copper, zinc, and gold are metals but are NOT magnetic. Only iron, nickel, cobalt and their alloys are strongly magnetic.
core_concepts.memory_tip: INC = Iron, Nickel, Cobalt — the only three purely magnetic elements. Everything else is non-magnetic. IRON rules magnetism.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: Every magnet has two poles — North (N) and South (S) — where the magnetic force is strongest. Like poles repel each other; unlike poles attract.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: The magnetic force of a bar magnet is strongest at its two ends, called poles. These are labelled North (N) and South (S). The North pole of a freely suspended magnet points towards geographic north; the South pole points south. Key law: like poles (N–N or S–S) repel each other, while unlike poles (N–S) attract. This is similar to electric charges (+ attracts –). A magnet's poles cannot be separated — if you cut a magnet in half, each half becomes a new complete magnet with both N and S poles (monopoles do not exist in classical physics).
core_concepts.real_life_example: If you try to push the N poles of two bar magnets together, they push away from each other (repulsion). But if you bring the N pole of one near the S pole of another, they snap together (attraction). This is visible with toy magnetic building blocks.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Magnetic levitation trains (Maglev) use repulsion between like poles to float above the track. ISRO Bengaluru uses precise magnetic sensors in satellite attitude control — these sensors rely on knowing exact pole orientations.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students confuse attraction with the rule — they think ALL magnets attract each other. In reality, two N poles or two S poles push each other away. Attraction only occurs between N and S poles.
core_concepts.memory_tip: POLES rule = Opposite Likes Enemies, Same = Enemies. N–S = best friends (attraction). N–N or S–S = enemies (repulsion). Just like people — opposites attract!

core_concepts.concept_name: Magnet as a Compass — Direction Finding
core_concepts.simple_explanation: A freely suspended magnet always points in the north–south direction. This property is used in a compass to find directions.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: When a bar magnet is suspended freely (hung from a thread or floated on water), it rotates until it aligns with Earth's magnetic field — North pole pointing approximately towards geographic north, South pole towards geographic south. This is because Earth itself acts like a giant magnet with magnetic poles near the geographic poles. A compass is simply a lightweight magnetised needle pivoted at its centre so it can rotate freely. The needle always points north, helping navigators find directions. Sailors and trekkers have used magnetic compasses for over a thousand years. Modern smartphones have electronic compasses (magnetometers) built in.
core_concepts.real_life_example: If you are lost in a forest and have a compass, the needle always points north. You then know which direction is east, west, and south by using north as your reference. Indian Railways and shipping use compasses for navigation even today.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: The Karnataka Forest Department and wildlife rangers in Nagarhole, Bandipur, and Bhadra tiger reserves use compasses during forest patrol. ISRO's Navigation Centre in Bengaluru uses magnetic and GPS-based navigation for spacecraft guidance. Mangaluru port navigation systems incorporate magnetic compasses as backup instruments.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students say the north pole of a compass needle points to Earth's North Pole — technically, the compass needle's North pole is attracted to Earth's geographic South magnetic pole (which is near geographic north). However, for school purposes, the standard answer is: the North pole of a magnet/compass points towards geographic north.
core_concepts.memory_tip: FREE magnet = compass. Suspend any magnet and it shows N–S. Earth is a giant magnet — it calls all smaller magnets to align with it. You + free magnet = instant compass.

core_concepts.simple_explanation: We can make magnets by stroking iron with a magnet or using electric current. Magnets lose their power when heated, dropped hard, or hammered.
core_concepts.detailed_explanation: Methods to make a magnet: (1) Single-stroke method — stroke an iron nail repeatedly in one direction with one pole of a bar magnet; after many strokes, the nail becomes a weak magnet. (2) Double-stroke (divided-touch) method — stroke with both poles simultaneously from the centre outward. (3) Electrical method — coil copper wire around an iron rod and pass electric current — this creates an electromagnet, which is magnetic only while current flows. An electromagnet is very useful because it can be switched on and off. Magnets lose their properties when: (a) dropped or struck hard (physical shock disturbs the alignment of magnetic domains), (b) heated strongly (thermal energy randomises domain alignment), (c) stored incorrectly without keepers (soft iron bars placed across poles).
core_concepts.real_life_example: A scrapyard uses a large electromagnet suspended from a crane — switch on the current and it lifts tonnes of scrap iron; switch off and the iron drops. MRI machines in hospitals use powerful electromagnets. The electric doorbell and electric motor use electromagnets.
core_concepts.karnataka_example: Hubballi-Dharwad's industrial zone manufactures small electric motors for agricultural pumps — all using electromagnet principles. BEML (Bharat Earth Movers Limited) in Bengaluru manufactures earth-moving equipment that uses electromagnets in electric motors. Karnataka's textile looms use electric motors built on electromagnetic principles.
core_concepts.common_mistakes: Students think once a magnet loses magnetism, it is permanently destroyed. This is not always true — a magnet made by the single-stroke method can be re-magnetised. Also, an electromagnet is only magnetic when current flows — students sometimes think it is always a magnet.
core_concepts.memory_tip: MAKE a magnet: Stroke + Same direction + One pole only. BREAK a magnet: Heat + Hit + Hammer. The three H's destroy magnets: Heat, Hit, Hammer.

key_vocabulary.definition: A material that attracts iron, nickel, and cobalt and has two poles
A material that is attracted by a magnet — e.g. iron, nickel, cobalt
A material not attracted by a magnet — e.g. wood, plastic, copper, aluminium
The two ends of a magnet (North and South) where magnetic force is strongest
The pulling force between unlike poles (N and S) of magnets
The pushing force between like poles (N–N or S–S) of magnets
A device with a magnetised needle that always points north, used to find direction
A naturally occurring magnetic rock (Fe₃O₄) — the first natural magnet discovered
A temporary magnet made by passing electric current through a coil of wire around an iron core
The region around a magnet where its magnetic force can be felt

questions.a: Iron, nickel, and cobalt are the three main magnetic materials.
Aluminium is non-magnetic. It is a metal but is not attracted by a magnet.

questions.q: You have a magnet and four objects: a steel spoon, a glass bottle, a copper wire, and an iron nail. Which will be attracted to the magnet?
questions.a: The steel spoon and the iron nail will be attracted. Glass and copper are non-magnetic.

questions.q: What happens when two North poles of two magnets are brought close?
questions.a: They repel each other — like poles repel.

questions.q: If you cut a bar magnet in half, how many poles will each piece have?
questions.a: Each half will have two poles — a North and a South pole. You cannot isolate a single pole.

key_takeaways: Magnets attract only magnetic materials: iron, nickel, cobalt, and their alloys like steel.
Aluminium, copper, wood, plastic, and rubber are non-magnetic.
Every magnet has two poles: North (N) and South (S). Magnetic force is strongest at the poles.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
A freely suspended magnet always points north–south — this is the basis of a compass.
Earth behaves like a giant magnet, causing all free magnets to align north–south.
Magnets can be made by stroking iron with a magnet or by using electric current (electromagnet).
Magnets lose their properties when heated, hammered, or dropped hard.
Electromagnets are temporary magnets — they work only when current flows.
Lodestone (magnetite) is a natural magnet; the legendary discovery involved a shepherd named Magnes.

must_remember_facts: Magnetic materials: iron, nickel, cobalt only (INC). Aluminium and copper are NOT magnetic.
Every magnet has exactly two poles — North and South. Poles cannot be separated.
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
A freely suspended magnet always points north–south.
A compass is a freely suspended magnetised needle used to find direction.
Earth acts like a giant magnet.
Electromagnet = iron core + wire coil + electric current; magnetic ONLY when current flows.
Magnets lose magnetism when heated, hammered, or dropped hard.
Lodestone (magnetite, Fe₃O₄) is a natural magnet.
Single-stroke method: stroke iron with one pole of a magnet, always in the SAME direction.
